rows.evidence: Q1: Material & method, Tentative layout <U+2013> a field experiment with three plots (T1 reclaimed water, T2 50% reclaimed water, C groundwater) under gravity drip irrigation of cucumber in 2011, with soil NH4-N and NO3-N sampled at 2, 5 and 9 days after irrigation and to 200 cm before and after the season (Figs. 1-3).
rows.notes: The study reports its own soil data: NH4-N rises in topsoil after reclaimed-water drip irrigation and returns to pre-irrigation level by day 9; NO3-N increases with soil depth (downward movement) and, for T1, rises by 38.20%, 44.67%, 34.94% and 30.88% in the 0-50, 50-100, 100-150 and 150-200 cm layers over the growing season, declining below 1.5 m. It does not measure groundwater, drainage or leachate; the statement that contaminants 'must' enter the groundwater system is an inference in the conclusion, not a measured result. The study therefore supports only a precondition (soil nitrate accumulation and downward distribution) of the claimed harm to groundwater. Also, the treatments compare water source (reclaimed vs groundwater) under drip, so the result is about reclaimed water rather than drip technology per se; drip is used but not compared against another irrigation method. No dispersion measures, no triangulation (one soil-extraction/flow-analyser method), single site, single season, three 4 m x 4 m plots, no stated limitations beyond generic calls for more research.
